From Middle Dutch totael, from Middle French total, from Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from tōtus (“all, whole, entire”).
Borrowed from Middle French tradition, from Old French tradicion, from Latin trāditiō, from the verb trādere.

From Middle Dutch translatie, borrowed from Middle French translation, from Latin trānslātiō (“transfer”), from trans (“across”), + lātiō (“carrying”), from lātus, perfect passive participle of irregular verb ferō (compare transfer), + noun of action suffix -iō.

From Middle Dutch transport, from Middle French transport, from Old French transport, from transporter (“to carry or convey across”), from Latin trānsportāre, from trāns- (“across, over, to the farther side of”) + portō (“to bear, carry, convey, take”).
Borrowed from Middle French terrasse, from Old Occitan. Doublet of terras.
Borrowed from Middle French train. The modern sense “railway vehicle” is a semantic loan from English train.

parole.significato: thick velvety fabric made of a cotton or linen weave and a wool or mohair pile, used in upholstery; Utrecht velvet
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tripe.
Borrowed from Middle French trivial, from Latin triviālis.

Borrowed from Middle French trouble, from Old French trouble, from Vulgar Latin *turbulus by metathesis. Displaced Middle Dutch torbel, from Old French torble, of the same source. Compare also German trüb, which might have reinforced the Dutch word.
Borrowed from Middle French trophée, from Latin trophaeum, variant of tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion).

parole.significato: a face, especially one with an unpleasant or unprepossessing look or expression; a mug
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch troenie, from Middle French trogne, possibly ultimately from a Celtic language, for which a Gaulish *trugna has been proposed (compare Welsh trwyn).

parole.significato: a tulip, a plant of the genus Tulipa
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tulipe, from Turkish tülbent (“fine muslin, turban”), from Persian دلبند (dolband, “turban”). Doublet of tulband.
Borrowed from Middle French tunique, from Latin tunica.
From Middle Dutch turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Old French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus.
From Middle French Turquoise, from Old French (pierre) turqueise (“Turkish (stone)”). The stone was originally brought to Europe from Turkestan.
Borrowed from Middle French unanime, from Latin unanimus.
Borrowed from Middle French union, from Latin ūniō.
Borrowed from Middle French uniforme, from Latin ūnifōrmis.
Borrowed from Middle French universel, from Latin ūniversālis.

parole.significato: vase, decorative pot or glass often used for containing severed branches or stems with flowers
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vase, from Latin vas.
Borrowed from Middle French vagabond, from Latin vagabundus.

parole.significato: variant, the act, process or instance of varying
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French variation, from Old French variacion, from Latin variātiō.
From Middle French varieté, from Latin varietās (“difference, diversity”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.

parole.significato: camp bed (lightweight portable bed used by the military, campers, etc.)
parole.testo: From veld + bed, calque of Middle French lit de camp.
Borrowed from Middle French vendue. First attested in the sixteenth century.
Borrowed from Middle French verbal, from Latin verbālis.

parole.significato: vermilion (orange-red colour; pigment or dye of this colour)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vermilioen, from Middle French vermillon.

parole.significato: vertical (perpendicular to the plane of the horizon)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vertical.
Borrowed from Middle French vestale.
Borrowed from Middle French viole, from Medieval Latin vitula. Doublet of vedel and viola.
Borrowed from Middle French vital, from Latin vītālis.

parole.significato: a high-ranking official or minister in an Islamic government, especially in the Ottoman Empire
parole.testo: From Middle French visir, from Ottoman Turkish وزیر (vezir), from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “helper, aide, minister”).
Borrowed from Middle French volume, from Old French volume, from Latin volūmen.

parole.significato: corrupt (lacking integrity, being prone to discriminating, open to bribes, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin corruptus or from Middle French corrupt.
16th century, either from Middle French démonstration or directly from Latin demonstratio. The sense “protest” is a 19th-century semantic loan from English demonstration.

Either from Middle Dutch depoost, from Middle French deposte, from Latin dēpositus, with adaptation of the spelling and pronunciation to Modern French dépôt, or borrowed anew from French dépôt, from the same Middle French word.

parole.significato: etymology (study of the origin and development of words)
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Middle French étymologie (from Old French ethimologie, from Latin) or directly a learned borrowing from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología).
Borrowed from Middle French exclusif, from Medieval Latin exclusivus. Alternatively, but less probably, directly borrowed from Mediaeval Latin.

From Middle Dutch paers, peers, pers (“purple”), from Middle French pers (“blue-grey, dark violet”), from Medieval Latin persus, persum (“dark blue”). Possibly derived from either Latin Persae (“Persians”), Persia (“Persia”), referring to the colour of a garment, or from Late Latin persica (“peach”)

Borrowed from Middle French pyramide, from Old French piramide, from Latin pȳramis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís), possibly from πῡρός (pūrós, “wheat”) + ἀμάω (amáō, “reap”) or from Egyptian pr-m-ws.
